question: An aerodynamic stall occurs when:

options.text: The airspeed drops below a fixed value printed in the aircraft's flight manual
The angle of attack exceeds the wing's critical (stalling) angle of attack, causing the airflow to separate
The engine loses power, regardless of angle of attack
The aircraft descends below its minimum safe altitude

explanation: A stall is fundamentally an angle-of-attack event, not an airspeed event: it occurs whenever the critical angle of attack is exceeded and the airflow separates from the upper surface, causing a sudden loss of lift. A published stalling speed is only the speed at which this angle is reached in one specific set of conditions.

question: In a level turn at a bank angle producing a load factor of 2g, how does the stalling speed compare with straight-and-level flight?

options.text: It is unchanged, since stalling speed does not depend on load factor
It increases by the square root of the load factor — about 1.41 times higher
It decreases, because the wings are generating more lift in the turn
It doubles exactly, in direct proportion to the load factor

explanation: Stalling speed increases in proportion to the square root of the load factor, because the wing must reach the same critical angle of attack at a higher speed to support the increased load. At 2g, stalling speed rises by the square root of 2, about 41%, over the 1g stalling speed.

question: If an aircraft's weight increases by 21% for a given flight, its stalling speed in the same configuration will:

options.text: Increase by approximately 10%, since stalling speed varies with the square root of weight
Increase by exactly 21%, in direct proportion to weight
Decrease, because a heavier aircraft requires a lower angle of attack
Remain unchanged, since stalling speed depends only on angle of attack

explanation: Because lift at the stall must equal weight, and lift varies with the square of speed at a fixed angle of attack, stalling speed varies with the square root of weight. A 21% increase in weight corresponds to a factor of the square root of 1.21, or 1.1 — an approximate 10% increase in stalling speed.

question: The purpose of a stall warning device, such as a stick shaker or an aural warning based on sensed angle of attack, is to:

options.text: Automatically recover the aircraft from a fully developed stall
Alert the pilot that the wing is approaching its critical angle of attack, before the stall actually occurs
Prevent the aircraft from descending below a set altitude
Indicate that the aircraft has exceeded its maximum operating speed

explanation: Stall warning systems are set to trigger at a small margin of angle of attack before the actual critical angle is reached, giving the pilot advance warning to reduce angle of attack before the stall develops. They warn of an approaching condition; they do not by themselves recover the aircraft.

question: Ice accumulation on the leading edge of a wing typically affects its stalling behaviour by:

options.text: Increasing the critical angle of attack and lowering the stalling speed
Having no aerodynamic effect until a significant thickness has built up
Disrupting airflow over the upper surface, which reduces the critical angle of attack and increases stalling speed
Only affecting drag, never lift or stall characteristics

explanation: Even small amounts of ice roughen and distort the leading edge, disturbing the smooth airflow needed to reach high angles of attack. This typically reduces the critical angle of attack at which the wing stalls and increases stalling speed, often with little warning from the aircraft's normal stall warning system.

question: Many wings are designed with "washout", a reduction in angle of incidence from root to tip, mainly so that:

options.text: The wingtip stalls before the wing root, keeping the ailerons effective for as long as possible
The wing root stalls before the wingtip, keeping the ailerons effective for as long as possible
Induced drag is eliminated entirely
The aircraft's cruise speed is increased

explanation: Washout gives the wing root a higher angle of attack than the tip at any given moment, so the root reaches its critical angle of attack and stalls first. This keeps the outboard section of the wing — and the ailerons mounted on it — flying and effective into the early stages of a stall.

question: An "accelerated stall" occurs when:

options.text: The aircraft stalls at a speed higher than the normal 1g stalling speed, due to a load factor greater than one, such as in a steep turn or abrupt pull-up
The aircraft stalls only at very low airspeed
The throttle is advanced to full power during the stall
The aircraft exceeds its never-exceed speed

explanation: "Accelerated" refers to the increased load factor, not to airspeed increasing: any manoeuvre that raises load factor above 1g raises the angle of attack needed to sustain it, so the critical angle of attack — and therefore the stall — is reached at a correspondingly higher airspeed.

question: A "secondary stall" is:

options.text: A stall that occurs a second time during the same flight, for unrelated reasons
A stall induced by an abrupt or premature recovery attempt from an initial stall, before sufficient airspeed has been regained
A stall that only affects the horizontal stabilizer
A stall from which recovery is never possible

explanation: A secondary stall happens when a pilot raises the nose again too soon during recovery from an initial stall, before the wing has regained enough airspeed to sustain the resulting angle of attack — stalling the wing a second time as a direct result of the recovery technique itself.

question: Which of the following is a typical aerodynamic symptom of an approaching stall, as distinct from an artificial stall warning device?

options.text: An increase in control effectiveness
Buffet caused by separated, turbulent airflow striking the tailplane or fuselage, and reduced control effectiveness
A sudden increase in airspeed
An automatic decrease in angle of attack

explanation: As the wing approaches its critical angle of attack, airflow begins separating naturally, and the resulting turbulent wake can buffet the tailplane or aft fuselage. Control surfaces immersed in this disturbed, slower-moving air also become less effective — both genuine aerodynamic warning signs, independent of any electronic or mechanical stall warning system.

question: An aerodynamic spin is best described as:

options.text: A rapid roll with the wings still flying normally
An autorotation following a stall, in which one wing is more deeply stalled than the other, combined with yaw
A steep spiral dive with the wings unstalled and airspeed increasing
A manoeuvre that can only happen at high airspeed

explanation: A spin requires the wing to already be stalled. One wing then becomes more deeply stalled than the other — often because of yaw at the stall — producing an asymmetric lift and drag condition that sustains a combined rolling, yawing, pitching autorotation, quite different from an unstalled spiral dive.

question: During the autorotative phase of a spin, the more deeply stalled, descending wing continues to auto-rotate mainly because:

options.text: It is producing more lift than the rising wing
Its effective angle of attack is even further past the stall, so it produces less lift and more drag than the rising wing, sustaining the rotation
Engine torque forces it downward
The ailerons are held fully deflected by the pilot throughout

explanation: The descending wing's downward motion adds to its angle of attack, driving it deeper into the stalled region of the lift curve where lift falls and drag rises further. The rising wing, meanwhile, sees a reduced angle of attack and produces relatively more lift and less drag — the asymmetry that keeps the rotation going on its own.

question: Aircraft with a T-tail configuration are particularly susceptible to a "deep stall" because:

options.text: The horizontal stabilizer is mounted low, ahead of the wing
At a high angle of attack, the turbulent, separated wake from the stalled wing can blanket the high-mounted horizontal stabilizer, severely reducing or eliminating elevator (pitch-down) authority
T-tails have no elevator at all
T-tails always stall at a lower angle of attack than a conventional tail

explanation: With the horizontal stabilizer mounted at the top of the fin, a sufficiently high angle of attack can place it directly in the wing's stalled, turbulent wake. If that happens, elevator authority to lower the nose can be badly degraded exactly when it is needed most — the mechanism behind a "deep stall" or "super-stall".

question: The fundamental first action in a standard stall recovery is to:

options.text: Apply full aft control input to raise the nose immediately
Reduce the angle of attack, typically by moving the control column forward (or reducing back-pressure), to unstall the wing before addressing power or altitude
Apply full rudder in the direction of the low wing
Retract the flaps immediately, regardless of airspeed

explanation: Because a stall is an angle-of-attack event, the only action that actually ends it is reducing angle of attack below the critical angle. Every other action — adding power, levelling the wings, managing altitude loss — matters, but comes after (or alongside) that first, essential step.

question: Compared with an aft center of gravity, a more forward center of gravity generally makes an aircraft:

options.text: More prone to entering and sustaining a spin
More resistant to stalling and spinning, though it also raises stalling speed slightly and requires more elevator authority to reach the critical angle of attack
Unaffected in its stall characteristics
Unable to stall at all

explanation: A forward center of gravity increases the tailplane's stabilising moment arm and generally makes the aircraft more resistant to reaching, and sustaining, a stalled or spinning condition — one reason aft CG limits exist. The trade-off is a slightly higher stalling speed and a greater elevator deflection needed to reach the critical angle of attack.
